questions.question_text: What happens if two threads call synchronized methods on the same object?
questions.answer: Only one of the two threads can execute at a time. Every object has one intrinsic lock (monitor). A thread must acquire that lock before entering any `synchronized` instance method of the object, so the second thread is blocked (moves to the BLOCKED state) until the first thread leaves its synchronized method and releases the lock. This holds even if the two threads call different synchronized methods of the same object, because they compete for the same monitor. If the threads use different objects, they do not block each other (static synchronized methods use the class-level lock instead).

questions.question_text: Why is multiple inheritance (through classes) not supported in Java?
questions.answer: Java does not allow a class to extend more than one class because of the diamond problem and the resulting ambiguity. If class C extended both A and B, and both defined (or inherited from a common ancestor) the same method or field, the compiler/JVM could not decide which version C should inherit, and constructor chaining would also become complicated. To keep the language simple and unambiguous, Java allows single inheritance of classes and obtains multiple inheritance of type through interfaces (a class can implement many interfaces, and any default-method conflict must be resolved explicitly by the implementing class).

questions.question_text: Explain the difference between commit() and rollback() in JDBC transactions.
questions.answer:
- `commit()` makes all the changes performed since the last commit/rollback in the current transaction permanent in the database (and releases the locks held). It is used once all statements of the transaction have executed successfully.
- `rollback()` undoes all the changes made in the current transaction (since the last commit or the given savepoint) and restores the database to its previous consistent state. It is typically called in the catch block when an error occurs.

Both are called on the `Connection` object and are meaningful only when auto-commit is disabled with `con.setAutoCommit(false)`.

Output:
```

```

Explanation: the `finally` block always executes before the method actually returns. When `return 10` is executed in the try block, the value 10 is held pending, but then the finally block runs and its own `return 30` overrides the earlier return, so the method returns 30. No exception occurs, so the catch block (return 20) is never executed.

A `return` inside `finally` discards any value returned from try/catch (and even swallows any exception thrown there), which is considered bad practice; compilers warn that 'finally block does not complete normally'.

questions.question_text: In the student race program, how can you use Thread.sleep() to simulate the running speed of students? Explain it with a two-student example.
Differentiate between Interface and abstract class. List any five significant dissimilarities.
questions.answer:
1. Methods: an interface declares abstract methods (plus `default`, `static` and `private` methods since Java 8/9); an abstract class can have both abstract methods and fully implemented (concrete) methods.
2. Variables: interface variables are implicitly `public static final` constants; an abstract class can have instance variables with any access modifier and non-final fields.
3. Inheritance: a class can implement multiple interfaces, but can extend only one abstract class (single inheritance).
4. Constructors: an interface cannot have constructors; an abstract class can have constructors (called through `super()` by subclasses).
5. Keywords/access: an interface is declared with `interface` and implemented with `implements`, and its methods are implicitly `public`; an abstract class is declared with `abstract class` and extended with `extends`, and its members may be `private`, `protected`, `public` or default.
6. Purpose: an interface defines a contract / capability (what a class can do) for unrelated classes; an abstract class represents a partially implemented base type (is-a relationship) sharing common state and code among closely related classes.
